title: Ξείνου βουλή
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Telemachus answers the stranger guardedly: his mother says he is the son of Odysseus, but no one can know his own father, and he would rather have been the son of a man who grew old at home among his possessions. Athena, still in the likeness of Mentes, assures him that his line will not be without a name, and asks what this crowd and this feast may be. Telemachus tells her. The house was prosperous while its master was at home, but the gods have made him vanish without trace, and the chief men of Ithaca and the neighbouring islands are wooing his mother, who neither refuses nor consents, while they eat up the household. Athena is indignant. She wishes Odysseus would appear at the door armed as she once saw him, on his way back from Ephyra, where Ilus son of Mermerus had refused him poison for his arrows and the father she claims as Mentes had given it; the suitors would soon be dead and their wooing bitter. His return rests with the gods, but she tells Telemachus what he can do: call an assembly and order the suitors home; let his mother go back to her father if she means to marry; take a ship to Pylos and Sparta and ask Nestor and Menelaus for news; if his father is alive, hold out for a year, and if he is dead, come home, raise his grave-mound and give his mother to a husband; then plan the suitors' deaths, by guile or openly, remembering the fame Orestes won by killing Aegisthus. Telemachus thanks her and presses her to stay for a bath and a guest-gift. She declines, asks him to keep the gift until she comes again, and flies off like a bird. Telemachus understands that a god has been with him, and goes back among the suitors with new courage.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A new whole-line formula of reply; it returns unchanged at 230 and 306. τήν is 'her': what looks like the article is in Homer a pronoun, and the narrator keeps the feminine for the goddess in a man's likeness. αὖ is 'in turn', the shorter form of αὖτε at 1.178. πεπνυμένος is the perfect participle of πέπνυμαι 'have one's wits about one, be prudent'; it is traditionally connected with πνέω 'breathe', though the link is not certain, and it is kept as 'prudent' every time. ἀντίον is an adverb, 'face to face, in answer'. ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak', with its augment (αὐ- lengthened to ηὐ-).

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, ξεῖνε, μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi, xeine, mal’ atrekeōs agoreusō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I will tell you, stranger, very exactly.
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you, stranger, quite exactly.
sentences.n: The line is Athena's own at 1.179, τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι ταῦτα μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύσω, with the vocative ξεῖνε where she had ταῦτα, and the English follows the rendering there. τοιγάρ, 'well then', takes up a request. τοι is the enclitic dative 'to you'. μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως answers her demand at 1.206–207 that he say exactly whether he is the son of Odysseus, and ἀγορεύσω is a future of promise. ξεῖνε is the vocative of ξεῖνος: he still takes his visitor for a stranger and a man.

sentences.t:
μήτηρ μέν τέ μέ φησι τοῦ ἔμμεναι, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ γε
οὐκ οἶδ’·
sentences.tr:
mētēr men te me phēsi tou emmenai, autar egō ge
ouk oid’·
sentences.l:
My mother says I am his, but I, for my part,
do not know;
sentences.i: My mother says that I am his; but I for my part do not know it,
sentences.n: μέν is answered by αὐτάρ, setting his mother's word against his own ignorance; the epic τε beside μέν has no English equivalent here. τοῦ is the article-form again as a pronoun, a genitive of origin, 'of him'. ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι): 'that I am his'. He does not name his father. ἐγώ γε, 'I at any rate', stresses the contrast. οὐκ οἶδ’, with οἶδ’ for οἶδα elided, is held over to the head of 216, where the edition ends the sentence with a raised point in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ πώ τις ἑὸν γόνον αὐτὸς ἀνέγνω.
sentences.tr: ou gar pō tis heon gonon autos anegnō.
sentences.l: for never yet has anyone by himself known his own begetting.
sentences.i: for no man has ever known of himself who fathered him.
sentences.n: The sentence gives the ground of his doubt as a general truth: no one knows his own parentage at first hand. ἀνέγνω is the aorist of ἀναγιγνώσκω 'know for certain, recognise', with its augment inside the compound (ἀν-έ-γνω). An aorist that states what is always so is called gnomic, and English turns it with a present or a perfect. ἑόν is from ἑός, a by-form of the possessive ὅς 'his own'. γόνος is 'birth, begetting, stock'. αὐτός is 'by himself'. πώ is 'yet'.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὴ ἐγώ γ’ ὄφελον μάκαρός νύ τευ ἔμμεναι υἱὸς
ἀνέρος, ὃν κτεάτεσσιν ἑοῖς ἔπι γῆρας ἔτετμε.
sentences.tr:
hōs dē egō g’ ophelon makaros ny teu emmenai huios
aneros, hon kteatessin heois epi gēras etetme.
sentences.l:
Would that I, for my part, were of some fortunate one the son,
a man whom among his own possessions old age overtook.
sentences.i: If only I were the son of some fortunate man whom old age came upon in the midst of his own possessions.
sentences.n: ὡς with ὄφελον and an infinitive is a wish that cannot now be fulfilled. ὄφελον is the aorist of ὀφείλω without its augment (Attic ὤφελον): Homer's past tenses may drop the ἐ-. The present infinitive ἔμμεναι makes the wish about the present, 'would that I were', and υἱός is nominative because the wisher is its subject. τευ is the epic genitive of the indefinite τις (Attic τινος). μάκαρ 'blessed' is of a man 'fortunate'. κτεάτεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι of κτέαρ 'possession', and in ἑοῖς ἔπι the preposition follows its noun and takes the accent. ἔτετμε, 'overtook', is a reduplicated aorist with its augment.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ὃς ἀποτμότατος γένετο θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων,
τοῦ μ’ ἔκ φασι γενέσθαι, ἐπεὶ σύ με τοῦτ’ ἐρεείνεις.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ hos apotmotatos geneto thnētōn anthrōpōn,
tou m’ ek phasi genesthai, epei sy me tout’ ereeineis.
sentences.l:
But as it is, he who became most ill-fated of mortal men,
from him they say I was born, since you ask me this.”
sentences.i: But as it is, the man who has proved the most ill-fated of mortal men — he is the one they say I was born from, since you ask me this.”
sentences.n: νῦν δέ is 'but as it is', the turn from wish back to fact. The relative clause comes first and its antecedent follows as τοῦ. τοῦ … ἔκ is ἐκ τοῦ, 'from him', with the preposition placed after its word and accented, as ἔπι was at 218. ἀποτμότατος is the superlative of ἄποτμος, ἀ- 'without' and πότμος 'lot, fate'. γένετο is unaugmented (Attic ἐγένετο). φασι, 'they say', takes up his mother's φησι at 215. ἐρεείνεις is from the epic ἐρεείνω 'ask'. Even now Telemachus does not speak his father's name. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The line is 1.178 word for word, and it keeps the English it has there. τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is one of the reply-formulas kept distinct in the English: in this part it stands beside τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα, which returns at 314, and the new formula of 213, whose αὖ is the shorter form of αὖτε 'in turn'. προσέειπε is the uncontracted aorist of προσεῖπον 'addressed'. θεά and γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη stand in apposition, 'the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena'; the exact sense of γλαυκῶπις is uncertain.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν τοι γενεήν γε θεοὶ νώνυμνον ὀπίσσω
θῆκαν, ἐπεὶ σέ γε τοῖον ἐγείνατο Πηνελόπεια.
sentences.tr:
ou men toi geneēn ge theoi nōnymnon opissō
thēkan, epei se ge toion egeinato Pēnelopeia.
sentences.l:
“Surely your lineage, at least, the gods have not made nameless hereafter,
since such a one as you Penelope bore.
sentences.i: “Surely the gods have not made your line one that will lack a name in time to come, since Penelope bore a son such as you.
sentences.n: οὐ μέν τοι is an emphatic denial: μέν is the affirming particle and τοι the particle 'I tell you', though τοι may also be taken as the dative 'for you'. γενεή, with Ionic η for Attic α, is 'birth, race, line'. νώνυμνος is 'nameless', νη- 'not' with ὄνυμα, an epic form of ὄνομα. ὀπίσσω, 'behind', is in Homer also 'hereafter'. θῆκαν is the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι (Attic ἔθηκαν), 'made', with a predicate adjective. ἐγείνατο, the aorist of γείνομαι 'bear', has its augment. Πηνελόπεια is named here for the first time in the poem. The goddess answers his doubt about his father by pointing to his mother.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον·
sentences.tr: all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon·
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: This is the line of 1.169 and 1.206, spoken now by Athena for the second time, and it keeps the same English; a repeated line keeps its rendering. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'come now', the imperative ἄγε used as an interjection. εἰπέ and κατάλεξον are aorist imperatives, and καταλέγω in Homer is 'recount in full and in order'. ἀτρεκέως, 'exactly', picks up Telemachus' μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως at 214: he has promised exactness, and she asks for it again on a new subject.

sentences.t: τίς δαίς, τίς δὲ ὅμιλος ὅδ’ ἔπλετο;
sentences.tr: tis dais, tis de homilos hod’ epleto;
sentences.l: What feast, what throng is this here?
sentences.i: What feast is this, what gathering?
sentences.n: τίς is used twice, once with each noun, and the verb comes only at the end. δαίς is a feast of shared portions, the word used of Poseidon's feast at 1.26. ὅμιλος is a crowd or throng of people. In δὲ ὅμιλος the δέ is left unelided before the vowel. ὅδ’ is ὅδε, 'this here', pointing at the hall. ἔπλετο is an aorist of πέλομαι 'be, become', used in Homer with the force of a present, 'is'. The visitor asks as though she did not know; the narrator showed her the suitors at 1.106–112.

sentences.t: τίπτε δέ σε χρεώ;
sentences.tr: tipte de se chreō;
sentences.l: And why ever is there need of it for you?
sentences.i: And what need do you have of it?
sentences.n: τίπτε is τί ποτε shortened, 'why ever, what then'. χρεώ is a noun, 'need', and σε is its object, 'what need is on you'; the verb is left unexpressed. The construction is related to that of χρή with an accusative of the person, which Telemachus used at 1.124 and which comes again at 296. She asks why the house should need such a feast at all, and the next line names the possibilities.

sentences.t: εἰλαπίνη ἠὲ γάμος;
sentences.tr: eilapinē ēe gamos;
sentences.l: A banquet, or a wedding?
sentences.i: Is it a banquet, or a wedding?
sentences.n: εἰλαπίνη is a festive banquet, generally taken to be one given by a single host; its derivation is uncertain. γάμος is a wedding, and so a wedding feast. ἠέ is the epic form of ἤ 'or'. The two nominatives stand with no verb, quick guesses at the answer. Each is a meal a host might give in his own house of his own accord, and the next clause rules out a third kind, the meal to which every guest contributes.

sentences.t: ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἔρανος τάδε γ’ ἐστίν·
sentences.tr: epei ouk eranos tade g’ estin·
sentences.l: since this, at least, is no meal of shared contributions;
sentences.i: It is certainly no meal where each man brings his share:
sentences.n: ἔρανος is a meal to which each of those taking part brings a contribution, as against a feast given by a host. ἐπεί gives the reason for her questions: the diners are plainly contributing nothing, so the meal must be of another kind. τάδε, 'these things', is the scene before her, and γε limits the claim to it: 'this, at any rate'. The raised point at the end of the clause leads into her account of how they are behaving.

sentences.t:
ὥς τέ μοι ὑβρίζοντες ὑπερφιάλως δοκέουσι
δαίνυσθαι κατὰ δῶμα.
sentences.tr:
hōs te moi hybrizontes hyperphialōs dokeousi
dainysthai kata dōma.
sentences.l:
so insolently and overbearingly, it seems to me, do they
feast throughout the house.
sentences.i: so insolent and overbearing they seem to me as they feast throughout the house.
sentences.n: ὥς τε is taken here as 'so, in such a way', with epic τε; it can also be read 'like men who', going with the participle, the comparative sense ὥς τε has at 308. The accent does not decide between them: it is thrown onto ὡς by the enclitic τε, not the accent of the adverb ὥς 'thus' at 1.6. ὑβρίζοντες is from ὕβρις, violent and insulting conduct towards others. ὑπερφιάλως, 'overbearingly', is the adverb of ὑπερφίαλος, the word used of the suitors at 1.134. δοκέουσι is uncontracted (Attic δοκοῦσι): Homer often leaves such vowels apart. μοι δοκέουσι is 'they seem to me'. δαίνυσθαι, 'to feast', is the verb of δαίς at 225. κατὰ δῶμα is 'throughout the house'.

sentences.t:
νεμεσσήσαιτό κεν ἀνὴρ
αἴσχεα πόλλ’ ὁρόων, ὅς τις πινυτός γε μετέλθοι.
sentences.tr:
nemessēsaito ken anēr
aischea poll’ horoōn, hos tis pinytos ge metelthoi.
sentences.l:
A man would be indignant,
seeing many shameful things, whoever of sense should come among them.”
sentences.i: Any man of sense who came among them would be indignant at the sight of so many shameful things.”
sentences.n: νεμεσσήσαιτο is an aorist optative with κεν, the epic ἄν: 'would be indignant'. It is the verb of Telemachus' own indignation at 1.119, with the double σ the verse wants there too; νέμεσις is the feeling that something improper is being done. αἴσχεα is the uncontracted plural of αἶσχος 'disgrace' (Attic αἴσχη). ὁρόων is ὁρῶν with the vowel stretched out. ὅς τις … μετέλθοι takes the optative of the main verb. πινυτός, 'sensible', is usually connected with the πεπνυμένος of 213. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The reply-formula of 213 returns word for word, and its English with it. τήν is again 'her', the narrator's feminine for the goddess in a man's likeness. πεπνυμένος is kept as 'prudent' whatever Telemachus is about to say, as a stock epithet is. In a line of this kind the name and epithet fill the middle of the verse, between τὴν δ’ αὖ and ἀντίον ηὔδα, and the speaker is fixed before a word of the speech is heard.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἐπεὶ ἂρ δὴ ταῦτά μ’ ἀνείρεαι ἠδὲ μεταλλᾷς,
μέλλεν μέν ποτε οἶκος ὅδ’ ἀφνειὸς καὶ ἀμύμων
ἔμμεναι, ὄφρ’ ἔτι κεῖνος ἀνὴρ ἐπιδήμιος ἦεν·
sentences.tr:
xein’, epei ar dē tauta m’ aneireai ēde metallāis,
mellen men pote oikos hod’ aphneios kai amymōn
emmenai, ophr’ eti keinos anēr epidēmios ēen·
sentences.i: “Stranger, since you do ask me this and inquire into it: this house was once on its way to being wealthy and blameless, as long as that man was still at home;
sentences.n: ξεῖν’ is ξεῖνε elided. ἂρ δή is 'since, as it seems, in fact'. ἀνείρεαι is the uncontracted second singular of ἀνείρομαι 'ask' (Attic -ῃ), and μεταλλᾷς is from μεταλλάω 'inquire after'. μέλλεν is the imperfect of μέλλω without augment; with the infinitive ἔμμεναι it says the house was on course to be rich. ἀμύμων is the stock epithet whose meaning is not known, rendered 'blameless' every time, here of a house. ὄφρα is 'as long as', not 'so that'. κεῖνος ἀνήρ, 'that man', again avoids the name. ἐπιδήμιος is 'at home', the word of 1.194, and ἦεν is ἦν.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἑτέρως ἐβόλοντο θεοὶ κακὰ μητιόωντες,
sentences.tr: nyn d’ heterōs ebolonto theoi kaka mētioōntes,
sentences.l: but now otherwise have the gods willed, devising evils,
sentences.i: but now the gods, devising evil, have willed it otherwise,
sentences.n: νῦν δέ turns from what was to what is, as at 219. ἐβόλοντο is the imperfect of βόλομαι, an epic form of βούλομαι, with its augment: 'the gods willed'. ἑτέρως is 'otherwise, the other way'. μητιόωντες is the participle of μητιάω 'devise, plan', from μῆτις 'counsel', with the vowel stretched out (Attic μητιῶντες). The unit ends at a comma because the sentence runs on for four more lines, and the relative οἳ that opens the next unit picks up θεοί.

sentences.t:
οἳ κεῖνον μὲν ἄιστον ἐποίησαν περὶ πάντων
ἀνθρώπων, ἐπεὶ οὔ κε θανόντι περ ὧδ’ ἀκαχοίμην,
εἰ μετὰ οἷς ἑτάροισι δάμη Τρώων ἐνὶ δήμῳ,
ἠὲ φίλων ἐν χερσίν, ἐπεὶ πόλεμον τολύπευσεν.
sentences.tr:
hoi keinon men aiston epoiēsan peri pantōn
anthrōpōn, epei ou ke thanonti per hōd’ akachoimēn,
ei meta hois hetaroisi damē Trōōn eni dēmōi,
ēe philōn en chersin, epei polemon tolypeusen.
sentences.l:
who that man have made unseen beyond all
men, since I would not grieve so for him even dead,
if among his own companions he had been laid low in the land of the Trojans,
or in the arms of his friends, after he had wound up the war.
sentences.i: who have made him vanish from sight more utterly than any other man; for I should not grieve so for him even if he were dead, had he fallen among his own companions in the land of the Trojans, or in the arms of his friends once he had wound up the war.
sentences.n: ἄιστος is ἀ- 'not' with the root of ἰδεῖν, 'unseen, vanished without trace'. περὶ πάντων ἀνθρώπων is 'beyond all men', περί with the genitive as at 1.66. ἀκαχοίμην is a reduplicated aorist optative of ἀκαχίζω 'grieve', and οὔ κε with it is 'I would not grieve'. θανόντι περ is 'for him, dead though he were', with concessive περ. δάμη is the unaugmented aorist passive of δάμνημι 'overpower' (Attic ἐδάμη). μετὰ οἷς ἑτάροισι has the possessive ὅς and a dative plural in -οισι. τολύπευσεν, unaugmented, is from τολύπη, a ball of spun wool: he 'wound up' the war.

sentences.t:
τῷ κέν οἱ τύμβον μὲν ἐποίησαν Παναχαιοί,
ἠδέ κε καὶ ᾧ παιδὶ μέγα κλέος ἤρατ’ ὀπίσσω.
sentences.tr:
tōi ken hoi tymbon men epoiēsan Panachaioi,
ēde ke kai hōi paidi mega kleos ērat’ opissō.
sentences.l:
Then for him a mound the Achaeans all together would have made,
and for his own son too great fame he would have won hereafter.
sentences.i: Then all the Achaeans would have raised a mound over him, and he would have won great fame for his son as well, in time to come.
sentences.n: τῷ is 'in that case, therefore'. κεν with an aorist indicative, ἐποίησαν and ἤρατ’, is 'would have' (Attic ἄν with the aorist indicative): what did not happen and might have. τύμβος is the burial mound raised over a dead man. Παναχαιοί is 'all the Achaeans' together. ᾧ παιδί is the possessive, 'for his own son'. ἤρατ’ is ἤρατο, an aorist middle 'won for himself', with the augment showing in ἠ-; the sense is that of ἀρνύμενος at 1.5. ὀπίσσω is 'hereafter', as at 222. The fame of a known death would have passed to the son.

sentences.t: νῦν δέ μιν ἀκλειῶς ἅρπυιαι ἀνηρείψαντο·
sentences.tr: nyn de min akleiōs harpuiai anēreipsanto·
sentences.l: But now, without fame, the Harpies have snatched him away;
sentences.i: But as it is, the Harpies have carried him off without fame;
sentences.n: ἀκλειῶς, 'without κλέος', stands against the μέγα κλέος of 240; it is the epic spelling of ἀκλεῶς. μιν is 'him'. ἅρπυιαι, printed in the edition as a common noun, are 'snatchers', from the root of ἁρπάζω; they are storm-winds pictured as beings that carry a man off so that he is never seen again. ἀνηρείψαντο is the aorist middle of ἀνερείπομαι 'snatch up and carry away', with the augment inside the compound (ἀν-ηρείψαντο, where ε is lengthened to η).

sentences.t:
οἴχετ’ ἄιστος ἄπυστος, ἐμοὶ δ’ ὀδύνας τε γόους τε
κάλλιπεν.
sentences.tr:
oichet’ aistos apystos, emoi d’ odynas te goous te
kallipen.
sentences.l:
he is gone, unseen, unheard-of, and for me pains and laments
he has left behind.
sentences.i: he is gone, unseen and unheard of, and for me he has left pain and weeping.
sentences.n: οἴχετ’ is οἴχεται, a present with the sense of a perfect, 'is gone'. ἄιστος ἄπυστος stand side by side with no 'and'. ἄπυστος is from the root of πυνθάνομαι, 'one of whom nothing is learned', and it pairs with ἄιστον at 235: no one has seen him, and no one has heard of him. ὀδύνας τε γόους τε is 'both pains and laments'. κάλλιπεν is κατέλιπεν: κατά is cut short, its τ assimilated to the λ that follows, and the aorist has no augment.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι κεῖνον ὀδυρόμενος στεναχίζω
οἶον, ἐπεί νύ μοι ἄλλα θεοὶ κακὰ κήδε’ ἔτευξαν.
sentences.tr:
oude ti keinon odyromenos stenachizō
oion, epei ny moi alla theoi kaka kēde’ eteuxan.
sentences.l:
Nor at all for that man, lamenting, do I groan
alone, since now for me other evil sorrows the gods have fashioned.
sentences.i: Yet it is not for him alone that I lament and groan, for the gods have fashioned other evil sorrows for me.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι is 'and not at all'. κεῖνον is the object of ὀδυρόμενος, and οἶον 'alone' is held over to the head of 244; with smooth breathing it is 'alone', not οἷον 'such as'. στεναχίζω is an epic present, 'groan'. νυ is the light particle 'now, as it is'. κήδε’ is κήδεα, uncontracted (Attic κήδη), 'sorrows, cares'. ἔτευξαν is the aorist of τεύχω 'make, fashion', with its augment. The next sentence says what the other sorrows are.

sentences.t:
ὅσσοι γὰρ νήσοισιν ἐπικρατέουσιν ἄριστοι,
Δουλιχίῳ τε Σάμῃ τε καὶ ὑλήεντι Ζακύνθῳ,
ἠδ’ ὅσσοι κραναὴν Ἰθάκην κάτα κοιρανέουσιν,
τόσσοι μητέρ’ ἐμὴν μνῶνται, τρύχουσι δὲ οἶκον.
sentences.tr:
hossoi gar nēsoisin epikrateousin aristoi,
Doulichiōi te Samēi te kai hylēenti Zakynthōi,
ēd’ hossoi kranaēn Ithakēn kata koiraneousin,
tossoi mēter’ emēn mnōntai, trychousi de oikon.
sentences.l:
For as many as hold power over the islands, the best men,
over Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus,
and as many as are lords throughout rocky Ithaca,
so many woo my mother, and wear out the house.
sentences.i: For all the chief men who hold power in the islands, in Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus, and all who are lords throughout rocky Ithaca — every one of them is wooing my mother and wearing out the house.
sentences.n: ὅσσοι … ὅσσοι … τόσσοι, 'as many as … so many', have the double σ the verse wants. ἐπικρατέουσιν is uncontracted, 'hold power over', with the dative νήσοισιν, and ἄριστοι, 'the best men', are the nobles. Dulichium, Same and Zacynthus are islands near Ithaca; where Dulichium lay is not known. ὑλήεις is 'wooded', as at 1.186. κραναός is 'rocky, rugged'. Ἰθάκην κάτα has the preposition after its noun and accented. κοιρανέουσιν is 'are lords'. μνῶνται is the verb of 1.39, 'woo'. τρύχουσι is 'wear out, exhaust'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ οὔτ’ ἀρνεῖται στυγερὸν γάμον οὔτε τελευτὴν
ποιῆσαι δύναται·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ out’ arneitai stygeron gamon oute teleutēn
poiēsai dynatai·
sentences.l:
And she neither refuses the hateful marriage nor an end
is able to make;
sentences.i: and she neither refuses the marriage she hates nor can bring the matter to an end;
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is the pronoun, 'and she', his mother. οὔτε … οὔτε balance the two things she does not do. ἀρνεῖται is 'refuses, says no to'. στυγερός is 'hateful', from στυγέω 'loathe': the marriage is hateful to her, and yet she does not refuse it. τελευτὴν ποιῆσαι, 'to make an end', is to settle the matter one way or the other. ποιῆσαι is the aorist infinitive with δύναται, held over to the head of 250.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ φθινύθουσιν ἔδοντες
οἶκον ἐμόν·
sentences.tr:
toi de phthinythousin edontes
oikon emon·
sentences.l:
and they waste away, by eating,
my house;
sentences.i: and meanwhile they are eating up my house and wasting it away;
sentences.n: τοί is the article-form as a pronoun, 'they', the suitors. φθινύθουσιν is an epic lengthened form of φθίνω, here transitive, 'waste, consume'. ἔδοντες is from the epic present ἔδω 'eat' (Attic ἐσθίω). οἶκον ἐμόν is held over to the head of 251. οἶκος is the house in the full sense, the household and all its stores, as in τρύχουσι δὲ οἶκον at 248.

sentences.t: τάχα δή με διαρραίσουσι καὶ αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: tacha dē me diarraisousi kai auton.
sentences.l: soon indeed they will shatter me, myself as well.”
sentences.i: and before long they will be the ruin of me too.”
sentences.n: τάχα is 'soon'. διαρραίσουσι is the future of διαρραίω 'break in pieces, destroy utterly', a compound of ῥαίω 'shatter'. καὶ αὐτόν is 'me myself as well': after the house, the man. The speech ends here, and the English layers close their quotation marks. It has moved from the lost father to the suitors, and from the suitors to the son's own danger.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐπαλαστήσασα προσηύδα Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ epalastēsasa prosēuda Pallas Athēnē·
sentences.l: To him, in deep indignation, spoke Pallas Athena:
sentences.i: Then Pallas Athena, stirred to indignation, spoke to him:
sentences.n: ἐπαλαστήσασα is the aorist participle of ἐπαλαστέω, a rare verb, 'be indignant, grieve bitterly at'. It is built on ἄλαστος 'not to be forgotten', said of a grief or a wrong that cannot be put out of mind, and the ἐπι- directs the feeling at what she has just heard. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω 'address', with its augment inside the compound (προσ-ηύδα). Παλλάς is a title of Athena whose meaning is not known.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ δὴ πολλὸν ἀποιχομένου Ὀδυσῆος
δεύῃ, ὅ κε μνηστῆρσιν ἀναιδέσι χεῖρας ἐφείη.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, ē dē pollon apoichomenou Odysēos
deuēi, ho ke mnēstērsin anaidesi cheiras epheiē.
sentences.l:
“Ah! truly, much do you lack Odysseus, gone away,
who would lay his hands upon the shameless suitors.
sentences.i: “Ah, truly you are much in want of Odysseus, gone away as he is, who would lay his hands on the shameless suitors.
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is an exclamation of surprise or displeasure. ἦ δή is 'truly now'. πολλόν is the epic πολύ, 'much'. δεύῃ is the second singular of δεύομαι, the epic form of δέομαι 'lack, need', with the genitive ἀποιχομένου Ὀδυσῆος. The goddess speaks the name Telemachus has avoided. ὅ is the article-form ὁ used as a relative, 'who', accented because the enclitic κε follows. κε with the optative ἐφείη, from ἐφίημι 'lay on', makes 'who would lay'. ἀναιδής is ἀν- 'without' with αἰδώς 'shame'.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ νῦν ἐλθὼν δόμου ἐν πρώτῃσι θύρῃσι
σταίη, ἔχων πήληκα καὶ ἀσπίδα καὶ δύο δοῦρε,
τοῖος ἐὼν οἷόν μιν ἐγὼ τὰ πρῶτ’ ἐνόησα
οἴκῳ ἐν ἡμετέρῳ πίνοντά τε τερπόμενόν τε,
sentences.tr:
ei gar nyn elthōn domou en prōtēisi thyrēisi
staiē, echōn pēlēka kai aspida kai dyo doure,
toios eōn hoion min egō ta prōt’ enoēsa
oikōi en hēmeterōi pinonta te terpomenon te,
sentences.l:
For if only now, having come, at the house's front doors
he would stand, holding a helmet and a shield and two spears,
being such as when I first set eyes on him
in our house, drinking and taking his delight,
sentences.i: If only he would come now and stand at the front doors of the house, with helmet and shield and two spears, just such a man as when I first set eyes on him in our house, drinking and taking his pleasure,
sentences.n: εἰ γάρ with the optative σταίη expresses a wish, 'if only he would stand'. πρώτῃσι θύρῃσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι, 'at the front doors'. σταίη is the aorist optative of ἵστημι. πήληξ is a helmet. δύο δοῦρε is a dual, 'two spears', from δόρυ with the epic stem δουρ-: Greek keeps a separate number for pairs. τοῖος … οἷον is 'such as'. τὰ πρῶτα is 'first'. ἐνόησα, 'caught sight of', is the aorist of νοέω with its augment. οἴκῳ ἐν ἡμετέρῳ is Mentes' house, part of the goddess's disguise.

sentences.t:
ἐξ Ἐφύρης ἀνιόντα παρ’ Ἴλου Μερμερίδαο—
ᾤχετο γὰρ καὶ κεῖσε θοῆς ἐπὶ νηὸς Ὀδυσσεὺς
φάρμακον ἀνδροφόνον διζήμενος, ὄφρα οἱ εἴη
ἰοὺς χρίεσθαι χαλκήρεας·
sentences.tr:
ex Ephyrēs anionta par’ Ilou Mermeridao—
ōicheto gar kai keise thoēs epi nēos Odysseus
pharmakon androphonon dizēmenos, ophra hoi eiē
ious chriesthai chalkēreas·
sentences.i: on his way back from Ephyra, from Ilus son of Mermerus — for Odysseus had gone there too on a swift ship, in search of a man-slaying drug, so that he might smear his bronze-fitted arrows with it;
sentences.n: ἀνιόντα, from ἄνειμι 'come back', agrees with μιν at 257. Ephyra is a name borne by several towns, and which one is meant is not certain. Μερμερίδαο is a genitive in -αο (Attic -ου) of the patronymic, 'son of Mermerus'. The dash opens an aside that runs to 264. ᾤχετο, 'had gone', is the imperfect of οἴχομαι with its augment (οἰ- becomes ᾠ-). θοός is 'swift', and νηός the epic genitive of ναῦς. φάρμακον is any drug, healing or deadly, and ἀνδροφόνον makes it poison. εἴη with the infinitive is 'it might be possible for him'. χαλκήρης is 'fitted with bronze'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν οὔ οἱ
δῶκεν, ἐπεί ῥα θεοὺς νεμεσίζετο αἰὲν ἐόντας,
ἀλλὰ πατήρ οἱ δῶκεν ἐμός·
sentences.tr:
all’ ho men ou hoi
dōken, epei rha theous nemesizeto aien eontas,
alla patēr hoi dōken emos·
sentences.i: but Ilus did not give it him, since he stood in awe of the gods who are forever; it was my father who gave it him,
sentences.n: ὁ μέν is the pronoun, 'he', Ilus, and ἀλλὰ πατήρ answers it. οἱ is 'to him', Odysseus, in both halves. δῶκεν is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι (Attic ἔδωκεν), used twice. νεμεσίζετο, an unaugmented imperfect, with the accusative is 'feared the anger of'; the line says only that he stood in awe of the gods, and implies that they would resent the poison. ῥα is the worn-down ἄρα. αἰὲν ἐόντας, 'who are forever', names the gods by what men lack. πατήρ … ἐμός is Anchialus, the father the goddess claimed at 1.180.

sentences.t:
φιλέεσκε γὰρ αἰνῶς—
τοῖος ἐὼν μνηστῆρσιν ὁμιλήσειεν Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr:
phileeske gar ainōs—
toios eōn mnēstērsin homilēseien Odysseus·
sentences.l:
for he loved him terribly —
being such, may Odysseus come among the suitors;
sentences.i: for he was exceedingly fond of him — if only Odysseus, being such a man as that, might come among the suitors!
sentences.n: φιλέεσκε is an iterative imperfect in -σκ-, 'he was fond of him', for what went on over a stretch of time; like most such forms it has no augment. αἰνῶς is 'terribly', here 'exceedingly'. The second dash closes the aside begun at 259, and 265 takes up the broken wish of 255 with the τοῖος ἐών of 257, 'being such a man'. ὁμιλήσειεν is an aorist optative of wish, still under εἰ γάρ. ὁμιλέω is 'be in company with', and it is also used of meeting in battle.

sentences.t: πάντες κ’ ὠκύμοροί τε γενοίατο πικρόγαμοί τε.
sentences.tr: pantes k’ ōkymoroi te genoiato pikrogamoi te.
sentences.l: all of them would become swift-doomed and bitter-wedded.
sentences.i: All of them would meet a swift doom and a bitter marriage.
sentences.n: κ’ is κε with the optative γενοίατο, 'would become', the consequence the wish has been leading to. γενοίατο has the epic third plural ending -ατο (Attic γένοιντο), like ἰδοίατο at 1.163. ὠκύμορος is ὠκύς 'swift' with μόρος 'portion, fate', 'early doomed'. πικρόγαμος is πικρός 'bitter' with γάμος 'marriage': the marriage they are after would turn bitter. τε … τε binds the two compounds, and both are kept hyphenated in the literal line to show how they are built.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι μὲν ταῦτα θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται,
ἤ κεν νοστήσας ἀποτίσεται, ἦε καὶ οὐκί,
οἷσιν ἐνὶ μεγάροισι·
sentences.tr:
all’ ē toi men tauta theōn en gounasi keitai,
ē ken nostēsas apotisetai, ēe kai ouki,
hoisin eni megaroisi·
sentences.i: But all this lies on the knees of the gods, whether or not he will come home and exact payment in his own halls;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι μέν turns from the wish to what can be known. θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται, 'lies on the knees of the gods', means that the outcome rests with them; the origin of the image is disputed. γούνασι is the epic dative plural of γόνυ (Attic γόνασι). ἤ κεν … ἦε is 'whether … or'. ἀποτίσεται is a future middle of ἀποτίνω, 'exact payment, take vengeance', the middle of the ἀπέτισεν of 1.43; the form could also be a short-vowel aorist subjunctive. οὐκί is an emphatic οὐ. οἷσιν is the possessive, 'his own'.

sentences.t:
σὲ δὲ φράζεσθαι ἄνωγα,
ὅππως κε μνηστῆρας ἀπώσεαι ἐκ μεγάροιο.
sentences.tr:
se de phrazesthai anōga,
hoppōs ke mnēstēras apōseai ek megaroio.
sentences.l:
but you I bid consider
how you are to thrust the suitors out of the hall.
sentences.i: but you, I bid you think how you are to drive the suitors out of the hall.
sentences.n: σὲ δέ answers ταῦτα μέν at 267: the gods have their part, and he has his. ἄνωγα is a perfect with the force of a present, 'I bid'. φράζεσθαι is the middle of φράζω, 'consider, think out'. ὅππως is ὅπως with the double π the verse wants. ἀπώσεαι, from ἀπωθέω 'thrust away', is uncontracted; with κε it may be a future or a short-vowel aorist subjunctive, and the form does not decide. μεγάροιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic μεγάρου), the hall where the suitors feast.

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἄγε νῦν ξυνίει καὶ ἐμῶν ἐμπάζεο μύθων·
sentences.tr: ei d’ age nyn xyniei kai emōn empazeo mythōn·
sentences.l: Come now, then, attend, and take heed of my words;
sentences.i: Come now, attend to me, and take heed of my words:
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἄγε is 'come now', with εἰ used as an interjection beside the imperative ἄγε. ξυνίει is the present imperative of ξυνίημι (= συνίημι), 'take in, attend', with ξυν- the epic form of συν-. ἐμπάζεο is the uncontracted present imperative middle of ἐμπάζομαι 'heed' (Attic ἐμπάζου), and it takes the genitive μύθων. The line turns from reflection to instructions, and its second half returns at 305 to close them.

sentences.t:
αὔριον εἰς ἀγορὴν καλέσας ἥρωας Ἀχαιοὺς
μῦθον πέφραδε πᾶσι, θεοὶ δ’ ἐπὶ μάρτυροι ἔστων.
sentences.tr:
aurion eis agorēn kalesas hērōas Achaious
mython pephrade pasi, theoi d’ epi martyroi estōn.
sentences.l:
Tomorrow, having called the Achaean heroes to assembly,
declare your word to all, and let the gods be witnesses to it.
sentences.i: Tomorrow call the Achaean heroes to assembly and declare your word to them all, and let the gods be witnesses.
sentences.n: εἰς ἀγορὴν καλέσας repeats the plan Athena put to the gods at 1.90, εἰς ἀγορὴν καλέσαντα: she now gives Telemachus the instruction herself. ἥρωες here are the nobles of Ithaca; in Homer the word is a general one for men of rank. πέφραδε is a reduplicated aorist imperative of φράζω 'point out, declare', the active beside the middle φράζεσθαι 'consider' at 269. ἐπί is an adverb, 'to it, over it'. μάρτυροι is an epic form of μάρτυρες, and ἔστων is the third plural imperative of εἰμί.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρας μὲν ἐπὶ σφέτερα σκίδνασθαι ἄνωχθι,
μητέρα δ’, εἴ οἱ θυμὸς ἐφορμᾶται γαμέεσθαι,
ἂψ ἴτω ἐς μέγαρον πατρὸς μέγα δυναμένοιο·
sentences.tr:
mnēstēras men epi sphetera skidnasthai anōchthi,
mētera d’, ei hoi thymos ephormatai gameesthai,
aps itō es megaron patros mega dynamenoio·
sentences.i: Order the suitors to scatter, each to his own home; and as for your mother, if her heart is set on marrying, let her go back to the hall of her father, a man of great power;
sentences.n: σφέτερα is 'their own', that is, their own homes. σκίδνασθαι is 'scatter, disperse'. ἄνωχθι is the perfect imperative of ἄνωγα, the verb of 269. The next clause changes construction: μητέρα is accusative as if it too were an object of ἄνωχθι, and then ἴτω, the third singular imperative of εἶμι 'go', takes over. οἱ is 'her'. ἐφορμᾶται is 'stirs, urges'. γαμέεσθαι is uncontracted; the middle of γαμέω is used of the woman, 'be married'. ἄψ is 'back'. Her father is not named here.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ γάμον τεύξουσι καὶ ἀρτυνέουσιν ἔεδνα
πολλὰ μάλ’, ὅσσα ἔοικε φίλης ἐπὶ παιδὸς ἕπεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hoi de gamon teuxousi kai artyneousin eedna
polla mal’, hossa eoike philēs epi paidos hepesthai.
sentences.l:
and they will make ready the marriage and prepare the wedding-gifts,
very many, as many as is fitting to go with a dear daughter.
sentences.i: and they will arrange the marriage and prepare wedding gifts in great number, as many as it is fitting should go with a dear daughter.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ, 'and they', are her father's people, not the suitors. τεύξουσι is the future of τεύχω 'make ready', and ἀρτυνέουσιν the uncontracted future of ἀρτύνω 'arrange'. ἔεδνα, with a prothetic ἐ- beside ἕδνα, are wedding gifts. The lexicons explain them as the gifts a suitor gives for his bride; here they are prepared by the bride's own family and go with her, and how the two fit together has long been discussed. ἐπί with the genitive παιδός is 'along with a daughter'. ἔοικε is 'it is fitting'.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ αὐτῷ πυκινῶς ὑποθήσομαι, αἴ κε πίθηαι·
sentences.tr: soi d’ autōi pykinōs hypothēsomai, ai ke pithēai·
sentences.l: And to you yourself I will shrewdly give counsel, if you will be persuaded:
sentences.i: And I will give shrewd counsel to you yourself, if you will be persuaded:
sentences.n: σοὶ δ’ αὐτῷ, 'and to you yourself', sets his own part against his mother's. ὑποθήσομαι is the future middle of ὑποτίθημι 'suggest, advise'. πυκινῶς is 'closely, shrewdly', from πυκινός 'close-packed', used of thought that is well put together. αἴ κε is the epic 'if' with κε, the equivalent of ἐάν; αἰ is the form of εἰ found in some dialects. πίθηαι is an uncontracted aorist subjunctive middle of πείθομαι 'be persuaded' (Attic πίθῃ).

sentences.t:
νῆ’ ἄρσας ἐρέτῃσιν ἐείκοσιν, ἥ τις ἀρίστη,
ἔρχεο πευσόμενος πατρὸς δὴν οἰχομένοιο,
ἤν τίς τοι εἴπῃσι βροτῶν, ἢ ὄσσαν ἀκούσῃς
ἐκ Διός, ἥ τε μάλιστα φέρει κλέος ἀνθρώποισι.
sentences.tr:
nē’ arsas eretēisin eeikosin, hē tis aristē,
ercheo peusomenos patros dēn oichomenoio,
ēn tis toi eipēisi brotōn, ē ossan akousēis
ek Dios, hē te malista pherei kleos anthrōpoisi.
sentences.l:
Fitting out a ship with twenty rowers, the best there is,
go to learn of your father, long gone,
in case some mortal tells you, or you hear a rumour
from Zeus, which most of all brings report to men.
sentences.i: Fit out the best ship there is with twenty oarsmen and go to learn of your father, so long gone, in case some mortal tells you, or you hear a rumour from Zeus, which more than anything carries news among men.
sentences.n: νῆ’ is νῆα, the epic accusative of ναῦς. ἄρσας is the aorist participle of ἀραρίσκω 'fit, equip'. ἐρέτῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσι, 'with rowers', and ἐείκοσιν the epic εἴκοσι. ἔρχεο is an uncontracted imperative (Attic ἔρχου). πευσόμενος is a future participle of purpose, as at 1.94. ἤν is ἐάν, with εἴπῃσι a subjunctive in -ῃσι. ὄσσα is a voice or rumour whose source no one knows, and so it is said to come from Zeus. κλέος here has its root sense, 'what is heard', report.

sentences.t:
πρῶτα μὲν ἐς Πύλον ἐλθὲ καὶ εἴρεο Νέστορα δῖον,
κεῖθεν δὲ Σπάρτηνδε παρὰ ξανθὸν Μενέλαον·
sentences.tr:
prōta men es Pylon elthe kai eireo Nestora dion,
keithen de Spartēnde para xanthon Menelaon·
sentences.l:
First go to Pylos and question heavenly Nestor,
and from there to Sparta, to fair-haired Menelaus;
sentences.i: Go first to Pylos and put your questions to heavenly Nestor, and from there to Sparta, to fair-haired Menelaus;
sentences.n: Nestor, lord of Pylos, and Menelaus, lord of Sparta and brother of Agamemnon, are named here for the first time in the poem. εἴρεο is the uncontracted imperative of εἴρομαι 'ask' (Attic ἔρου). δῖος is 'heavenly', the epithet of Odysseus at 1.196, kept the same for Nestor. κεῖθεν is ἐκεῖθεν, with the suffix -θεν 'from', and Σπάρτηνδε has -δε 'to'. ξανθός is a colour-word, yellow to light brown, used of hair; the English 'fair-haired' supplies the hair. πρῶτα μέν … κεῖθεν δέ set out the order of the journey.

sentences.t: ὃς γὰρ δεύτατος ἦλθεν Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων.
sentences.tr: hos gar deutatos ēlthen Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn.
sentences.l: for he came back last of the bronze-shirted Achaeans.
sentences.i: for he was the last of the bronze-shirted Achaeans to come home.
sentences.n: ὅς here is a demonstrative, 'he', not a relative: ὃς γάρ is 'for he'. δεύτατος is a superlative formed from δεύτερος, 'last'. ἦλθεν, 'came', is understood as came home from Troy. χαλκοχίτων is χαλκός 'bronze' with χιτών 'tunic', 'with tunics of bronze', an epithet of the Achaeans, and the English keeps the garment. The last man home has the freshest news, and that is the reason given for sending Telemachus to him.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν κεν πατρὸς βίοτον καὶ νόστον ἀκούσῃς,
ἦ τ’ ἂν τρυχόμενός περ ἔτι τλαίης ἐνιαυτόν·
sentences.tr:
ei men ken patros bioton kai noston akousēis,
ē t’ an trychomenos per eti tlaiēs eniauton·
sentences.l:
If you hear of your father's life and homecoming,
then truly, worn down though you are, you could endure yet a year;
sentences.i: If you hear that your father is alive and on his way home, then, worn down as you are, you could still hold out for another year;
sentences.n: εἰ … κεν with the aorist subjunctive ἀκούσῃς is the epic equivalent of ἐάν. βίοτον καὶ νόστον, 'life and homecoming', means that he is alive and on his way. ἦ τ’ ἄν is 'then surely', with ἄν, which Homer uses beside κε. τλαίης is an aorist optative from the root of τλῆναι 'endure', the root of ταλασίφρων: 'you could bear'. τρυχόμενος is the passive of τρύχω, the verb Telemachus used at 248 of the suitors wearing out the house; now he himself is the one worn down. ἐνιαυτόν is an accusative of time.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε τεθνηῶτος ἀκούσῃς μηδ’ ἔτ’ ἐόντος,
νοστήσας δὴ ἔπειτα φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν
σῆμά τέ οἱ χεῦαι καὶ ἐπὶ κτέρεα κτερεΐξαι
πολλὰ μάλ’, ὅσσα ἔοικε, καὶ ἀνέρι μητέρα δοῦναι.
sentences.tr:
ei de ke tethnēōtos akousēis mēd’ et’ eontos,
nostēsas dē epeita philēn es patrida gaian
sēma te hoi cheuai kai epi kterea ktereïxai
polla mal’, hossa eoike, kai aneri mētera dounai.
sentences.l:
But if you hear that he is dead and no longer living,
then, returning to your dear fatherland,
heap up a mound for him, and pay the funeral-honours besides,
very many, as many as is fitting, and give your mother to a husband.
sentences.i: But if you hear that he is dead and gone, then come home to your dear fatherland, heap up a mound for him and pay him funeral honours in full, as many as are fitting, and give your mother to a husband.
sentences.n: τεθνηῶτος is the epic perfect participle of θνῄσκω (Attic τεθνεῶτος), a genitive with ἀκούσῃς 'hear of'. μηδ’ ἔτ’ ἐόντος is 'and no longer being'. φίλην … πατρίδα γαῖαν is rendered as φίλη πατρὶς αἶα is, 'dear fatherland'. χεῦαι, κτερεΐξαι and δοῦναι are aorist infinitives used as imperatives. σῆμα is a sign, here the mound that marks a grave. κτέρεα κτερεΐξαι, noun and verb of one root, is 'pay the funeral honours'; ἐπί is an adverb, 'besides'. πολλὰ μάλ’, ὅσσα ἔοικε repeats the words of 278. ἀνέρι is 'to a husband'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπὴν δὴ ταῦτα τελευτήσῃς τε καὶ ἔρξῃς,
φράζεσθαι δὴ ἔπειτα κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμὸν
ὅππως κε μνηστῆρας ἐνὶ μεγάροισι τεοῖσι
κτείνῃς ἠὲ δόλῳ ἢ ἀμφαδόν·
sentences.tr:
autar epēn dē tauta teleutēsēis te kai erxēis,
phrazesthai dē epeita kata phrena kai kata thymon
hoppōs ke mnēstēras eni megaroisi teoisi
kteinēis ēe dolōi ē amphadon·
sentences.l:
But when you have finished these things and done them,
then consider in mind and in heart
how you may kill the suitors in your halls,
either by guile or openly;
sentences.i: And when you have finished all this and done it, then consider in your mind and heart how you may kill the suitors in your halls, whether by guile or in the open;
sentences.n: ἐπήν is ἐπεὶ ἄν, 'when', with the aorist subjunctives τελευτήσῃς and ἔρξῃς; ἔρξῃς is from ἔρδω, the same verb as ῥέζω. φράζεσθαι is another infinitive used as an imperative, the verb of 269. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν, 'in mind and in heart', pairs the seat of thought with the seat of feeling. τεοῖσι is the epic τεός 'your' (Attic σοῖς) with a dative in -οισι. κτείνῃς is a present subjunctive. δόλῳ 'by guile' and ἀμφαδόν 'openly' are the two ways, and the goddess does not choose between them.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
νηπιάας ὀχέειν, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι τηλίκος ἐσσι.
sentences.tr:
oude ti se chrē
nēpiaas ocheein, epei ouketi tēlikos essi.
sentences.l:
and there is no need for you
to carry on childish ways, since you are no longer of that age.
sentences.i: it is not right for you to keep up the ways of a child, for you are no longer of an age for that.
sentences.n: χρή takes the accusative σε with the infinitive, 'it is needful for you'. νηπιάας is an accusative plural, 'childish ways', from νηπιέη, the noun of νήπιος 'child, fool', the word used of the companions at 1.8. ὀχέειν is uncontracted, 'carry, keep up'. τηλίκος is 'of such an age', that is, of a child's age. ἐσσι is the epic second singular of εἰμί (Attic εἶ). The sentence begins in the middle of 296, after the raised point, and ends the practical advice.

sentences.l:
Or do you not hear what fame heavenly Orestes won
among all men, when he killed his father's slayer,
Aegisthus of guileful counsel, who had killed his famous father?
sentences.i: Or have you not heard what fame heavenly Orestes won among all men when he killed the slayer of his father, Aegisthus of guileful counsel, who had killed his famous father?
sentences.n: ἤ introduces an indignant question, 'or have you not heard?'. ἀίεις is the present of ἀίω 'hear, perceive'. ἔλλαβε is the aorist of λαμβάνω with its augment and a double λ (Attic ἔλαβε). δῖος is 'heavenly' by the house rule, here of Orestes. πατροφονῆα is the accusative of πατροφονεύς 'father-slayer' (Attic -έα). δολόμητις, δόλος 'guile' with μῆτις 'counsel', is a new epithet for the man called ἀμύμων at 1.29, and δόλῳ at 296 has just named guile. ὅ is the article-form as a relative, 'who', accented before the enclitic οἱ. ἔκτανε and ἔκτα are two forms of the aorist of κτείνω.

sentences.t:
καὶ σύ, φίλος, μάλα γάρ σ’ ὁρόω καλόν τε μέγαν τε,
ἄλκιμος ἔσσ’, ἵνα τίς σε καὶ ὀψιγόνων ἐὺ εἴπῃ.
sentences.tr:
kai sy, philos, mala gar s’ horoō kalon te megan te,
alkimos ess’, hina tis se kai opsigonōn ey eipēi.
sentences.l:
You too, friend — for very much I see you fine and tall —
be valiant, so that someone even of those born later may speak well of you.
sentences.i: You too, my friend — for I see that you are very fine and tall — be brave, so that men born long after may speak well of you.
sentences.n: φίλος is a nominative used as a vocative, 'friend'. μάλα γάρ … μέγαν τε is a parenthesis. ὁρόω is ὁρῶ with the vowel stretched out. καλόν τε μέγαν τε is 'fine and tall'. ἔσσ’ is ἔσσο, the epic imperative of εἰμί (Attic ἴσθι). ἄλκιμος is 'strong in defence, valiant', from ἀλκή; the same adjective was used of Athena's spear at 1.99. ἵνα with the subjunctive εἴπῃ is a purpose clause. ὀψίγονοι are 'the late-born', men of later generations, and καί makes it 'even'. ἐὺ εἴπῃ is 'speak well of'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν κατελεύσομαι ἤδη
ἠδ’ ἑτάρους, οἵ πού με μάλ’ ἀσχαλόωσι μένοντες·
sentences.tr:
autar egōn epi nēa thoēn kateleusomai ēdē
ēd’ hetarous, hoi pou me mal’ aschaloōsi menontes·
sentences.l:
But I will go down now to my swift ship
and my companions, who, I suppose, are chafing greatly as they wait for me;
sentences.i: But now I will go down to my swift ship and my companions, who must be growing very impatient waiting for me;
sentences.n: ἐγών is ἐγώ before a vowel, as at 1.88. νῆα θοήν is the 'swift ship' of 260, now in the accusative. κατελεύσομαι is the future of κατέρχομαι, 'go down', from the house to the shore. ἤδη is 'now, at once'. ἑτάρους, like νῆα, depends on ἐπί. πού is 'I suppose'. ἀσχαλόωσι is ἀσχαλῶσι stretched out, 'chafe, are vexed', and με is the object of μένοντες, 'waiting for me'. The ship and crew belong to the story of 1.182–186.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ αὐτῷ μελέτω, καὶ ἐμῶν ἐμπάζεο μύθων.
sentences.tr: soi d’ autōi meletō, kai emōn empazeo mythōn.
sentences.l: and to you yourself let it be a care, and take heed of my words.”
sentences.i: let this be your own concern, and take heed of my words.”
sentences.n: μελέτω is the third singular imperative of μέλω 'be a care', the verb of 1.159, with the dative σοὶ … αὐτῷ, which repeats the opening words of 279. The second half of the line is the second half of 271, and it closes the instructions as that line opened them. The speech ends here, and the English layers close their quotation marks. It has run from 253, fifty-three lines, the longest speech in the poem so far.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To her in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to her in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The reply-formula of 213 and 230 returns for the third time in this part, with the same English. αὖ 'in turn' marks the change of speaker. πεπνυμένος stays 'prudent': the epithet goes with the man, as the house rule for stock epithets requires. ἀντίον is 'face to face', and ηὔδα 'spoke'.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἦ τοι μὲν ταῦτα φίλα φρονέων ἀγορεύεις,
ὥς τε πατὴρ ᾧ παιδί, καὶ οὔ ποτε λήσομαι αὐτῶν.
sentences.tr:
xein’, ē toi men tauta phila phroneōn agoreueis,
hōs te patēr hōi paidi, kai ou pote lēsomai autōn.
sentences.l:
“Stranger, truly you speak these things with friendly mind,
as a father to his own son, and never will I forget them.
sentences.i: “Stranger, you speak all this out of kindness, as a father would to his own son, and I shall never forget it.
sentences.n: ξεῖν’ is ξεῖνε elided, as at 231. ἦ τοι μέν is 'truly'. φίλα φρονέων, 'thinking friendly things', is 'meaning well', the same turn as ἀγαθὰ φρονέων said of Hermes at 1.43; φρονέων is uncontracted. ὥς τε, 'just as', introduces a comparison with the verb understood. ᾧ παιδί has the possessive ὅς, 'to his own son'. λήσομαι is the future of λανθάνομαι 'forget', with the genitive αὐτῶν. A son without a father at hand hears the stranger's counsel as a father's.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν ἐπίμεινον, ἐπειγόμενός περ ὁδοῖο,
sentences.tr: all’ age nyn epimeinon, epeigomenos per hodoio,
sentences.l: But come now, wait a while, eager though you are for your way,
sentences.i: But come now, stay a while, eager as you are to be on your way,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν is 'but come now'. ἐπίμεινον is the aorist imperative of ἐπιμένω 'wait, stay on'. ἐπειγόμενος is 'pressing on, in haste', with the genitive ὁδοῖο, 'for the road', a genitive in -οιο of ὁδός. περ with the participle is concessive, as at 236. The unit ends at a comma because the sentence runs on through 313, five lines in all. The host's duty is to keep a guest long enough to honour him.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα λοεσσάμενός τε τεταρπόμενός τε φίλον κῆρ,
δῶρον ἔχων ἐπὶ νῆα κίῃς, χαίρων ἐνὶ θυμῷ,
τιμῆεν, μάλα καλόν, ὅ τοι κειμήλιον ἔσται
ἐξ ἐμεῦ, οἷα φίλοι ξεῖνοι ξείνοισι διδοῦσι.
sentences.tr:
ophra loessamenos te tetarpomenos te philon kēr,
dōron echōn epi nēa kiēis, chairōn eni thymōi,
timēen, mala kalon, ho toi keimēlion estai
ex emeu, hoia philoi xeinoi xeinoisi didousi.
sentences.l:
so that, having bathed and taken your fill in your own heart,
you may go to your ship holding a gift, rejoicing in your spirit,
a precious one, very fine, which will be a treasure for you
from me, such as dear guest-friends give to guest-friends.”
sentences.i: so that you may bathe and take your fill of pleasure, and then go to your ship glad at heart with a gift, a precious one and very fine, which will be a treasure for you from me, the kind of gift that dear guest-friends give to their guest-friends.”
sentences.n: ὄφρα is 'so that' here, with the subjunctive κίῃς from κίω 'go'. λοεσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of λούω 'bathe', with the epic stem λοε- and double σ. τεταρπόμενος is a reduplicated aorist middle participle of τέρπω, 'having taken your fill', with φίλον κῆρ an accusative of respect, 'in your own heart'. τιμῆεν is contracted from τιμήεις 'precious'. κειμήλιον, from κεῖμαι, is a thing laid by, a treasure kept in the house. ἐξ ἐμεῦ is 'from me' (Attic ἐμοῦ). ξεῖνοι here are guest-friends, as at 1.187. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Him then answered the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, answered him:
sentences.n: The line is 1.44 and 1.80 word for word, and it keeps the English it has there. After τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε at 221, the other formula for Athena's replies returns: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα, 'him then answered', with ἠμείβετ’ the imperfect middle of ἀμείβω, in the middle 'answer'. The noun of the same root, ἀμοιβή 'return, exchange', closes her reply at 318.

sentences.t: μή μ’ ἔτι νῦν κατέρυκε, λιλαιόμενόν περ ὁδοῖο.
sentences.tr: mē m’ eti nyn kateryke, lilaiomenon per hodoio.
sentences.l: “Do not hold me back any longer now, eager as I am for my way.
sentences.i: “Do not keep me here any longer now, eager as I am to be on my way.
sentences.n: μή with the present imperative κατέρυκε forbids what is going on: 'stop holding me back'. κατερύκω is the verb used of Calypso keeping Odysseus at 1.55. μ’ is με. λιλαιόμενον is masculine: the goddess speaks of herself as the man she seems to be. λιλαιόμενόν περ ὁδοῖο answers Telemachus' ἐπειγόμενός περ ὁδοῖο at 309, in the same place at the end of the line, so that she turns his own words back to him.

sentences.t:
δῶρον δ’ ὅττι κέ μοι δοῦναι φίλον ἦτορ ἀνώγῃ,
αὖτις ἀνερχομένῳ δόμεναι οἶκόνδε φέρεσθαι,
καὶ μάλα καλὸν ἑλών·
sentences.tr:
dōron d’ hotti ke moi dounai philon ētor anōgēi,
autis anerchomenōi domenai oikonde pheresthai,
kai mala kalon helōn·
sentences.i: As for the gift, whatever your heart bids you give me, give it when I come back this way, to take home with me, and choose a very fine one;
sentences.n: δῶρον is set first as the topic. ὅττι κε with the subjunctive ἀνώγῃ is 'whatever … may bid'; φίλον ἦτορ is 'your own heart', as at 1.60. δοῦναι and δόμεναι, 'to give', stand in consecutive lines: the first is the ordinary form, the second the epic infinitive in -μεναι, here used as an imperative. ἀνερχομένῳ is masculine again, 'to me as I come back'. οἶκόνδε has -δε 'to', and φέρεσθαι is the middle, 'to carry off for myself'. ἑλών, 'picking out', is nominative and refers to Telemachus.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ ἄξιον ἔσται ἀμοιβῆς.
sentences.tr: soi d’ axion estai amoibēs.
sentences.l: and to you it will be worth a return.”
sentences.i: and it will bring you its worth in return.”
sentences.n: The subject is the gift. ἄξιος with the genitive is 'worth', and ἀμοιβή, from ἀμείβω, is 'exchange, return': the gift will be worth one given back of equal value, since guest-gifts were given in exchange. σοὶ δ’ is 'and for you'. ἔσται is the ordinary future of εἰμί, beside the epic ἔσσεται of 1.40. The speech ends here, and the English layers close their quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἀπέβη γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
ὄρνις δ’ ὣς ἀνόπαια διέπτατο·
sentences.tr:
hē men ar’ hōs eipous’ apebē glaukōpis Athēnē,
ornis d’ hōs anopaia dieptato·
sentences.l:
She then, so having spoken, went away, gleaming-eyed Athena,
and like a bird, upward, she flew off;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and gleaming-eyed Athena went away, and like a bird she flew off upward;
sentences.n: ἡ μέν is the pronoun, 'she', with ἄρ’ (= ἄρα) 'then'. ὣς εἰποῦσ’ is the phrase of 1.96. ὄρνις δ’ ὥς is 'like a bird', with ὥς after its noun and accented. The meaning of ἀνόπαια is disputed: ancient readers took it as 'upward' or as 'unseen', or divided it as ἀν’ ὀπαῖα 'up through the smoke-vent', or made it the name of a kind of bird. ἀπέβη and διέπτατο are aorists of ἀποβαίνω and διαπέτομαι 'fly off', each with the augment inside the compound (ἀπ-έ-βη, δι-έ-πτατο). Whether she takes a bird's shape or only flies like one, the Greek does not settle.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
θῆκε μένος καὶ θάρσος, ὑπέμνησέν τέ ἑ πατρὸς
μᾶλλον ἔτ’ ἢ τὸ πάροιθεν.
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ eni thymōi
thēke menos kai tharsos, hypemnēsen te he patros
mallon et’ ē to paroithen.
sentences.l:
and in him, in his heart,
she put force and courage, and made him mindful of his father
still more than before.
sentences.i: and in his heart she put force and courage, and turned his thoughts to his father even more than before.
sentences.n: τῷ is the pronoun, 'in him', with ἐνὶ θυμῷ 'in his heart'. θῆκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι. μένος is the force Athena said at 1.89 she would put in the son's mind; what she planned there is done here. θάρσος is 'boldness, courage'. ὑπέμνησεν is the aorist of ὑπομιμνῄσκω 'remind', with its augment inside the compound (ὑπ-έ-μνησεν), and it takes a genitive of what is recalled, πατρός. ἑ is the epic accusative 'him' (Attic αὐτόν). τὸ πάροιθεν is 'before'.

sentences.t:
ὁ δὲ φρεσὶν ᾗσι νοήσας
θάμβησεν κατὰ θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
ho de phresin hēisi noēsas
thambēsen kata thymon·
sentences.l:
And he, perceiving it in his own mind,
was amazed in his heart;
sentences.i: And he understood it in his mind, and was struck with wonder in his heart;
sentences.n: ὁ δέ is the pronoun, 'and he'. φρεσὶν ᾗσι has the possessive ὅς in the dative plural, 'in his own mind'. νοήσας is the aorist participle of νοέω 'perceive, understand', the verb Athena used at 257 of first seeing Odysseus. θάμβησεν is the unaugmented aorist of θαμβέω 'be astonished' (Attic ἐθάμβησεν). φρένες and θυμός stand side by side here, as they did at 294 in the goddess's advice.

sentences.t: ὀίσατο γὰρ θεὸν εἶναι.
sentences.tr: oisato gar theon einai.
sentences.l: for he thought it was a god.
sentences.i: for he believed that it had been a god.
sentences.n: ὀίσατο is the aorist of ὀίομαι 'think, suppose', without augment. The subject of the infinitive, the visitor, is left unexpressed, and θεόν is its predicate: 'that it was a god'. He does not know which god; the reader has known all along. The half-line gives the reason for his amazement in four words.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δὲ μνηστῆρας ἐπῴχετο ἰσόθεος φώς.
sentences.tr: autika de mnēstēras epōicheto isotheos phōs.
sentences.l: And at once he went among the suitors, a man equal to a god.
sentences.i: And at once he went among the suitors, a man the equal of a god.
sentences.n: αὐτίκα is 'at once'. ἐπῴχετο is the imperfect of ἐποίχομαι 'go to, go among', with its augment inside the compound (ἐπ-ῴχετο); it is the verb used of the herald at 1.143. ἰσόθεος is ἴσος 'equal' with θεός, and φώς is a poetic word for 'man'. The epithet is new to the poem, and it is kept apart from ἀντίθεος 'godlike' and θεοειδής 'godlike in form'. It stands one line after θεόν: he has just recognised a god, and the narrator calls him the equal of one.
